newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Villiger says Swiss govt to continue cost cuts.
newsitem.headline: Villiger says Swiss govt to continue cost cuts.

text.p: Swiss finance minister Kaspar Villiger said the economy was still lagging but the federal government would continue its cost-cutting efforts.
He expected the economy to show a slow recovery by mid-year.

"I believe that the economy will soon bottom out, and that around the middle of the year we could start to see a recovery," he said in the text of a speech to be delivered before the Statistical-Economic Society.
But he said the government's finances and the economy would still face challenges.

"A real change in the trend is still not in sight. But in any case, the budget for 1997 remains on the same nominal level as that of 1996, and the finance plan for 1998-2000 has been stabilised on a real basis."
He said the federal deficit is now estimated at between 5.0 billion and 6.0 billion Swiss francs annually, despite significant cost-cutting measures.

But these figures were based on an outlook for an optimistic economic performance, and every percentage point reduction in growth below estimate would raise the deficit by 500 million francs, irrespective of unemployment insurance.

Arguments that the government should first try to boost the economy with a more expansive fiscal policy, and cut costs later, should not be misused for political purposes to provide subsidies which are no longer justified, Villiger said.

Villiger said several tasks remain to revitalise the economy, which economists say is suffering from a structural malaise. These included restructuring the federal railways, modernising corporate tax structures, further opening markets such as energy, concluding talks bilateral with the European Union, consolidating social security and revamping federal finances, Villiger said.

Last week the Swiss economics ministry said it was seeking to launch a 550 million Swiss franc economic stimulus package, providing Swiss Cantons and local governments also agree to increase spending.

In late European trade, currency market traders said that the dollar rose after comments Villiger made in an interview in Berne earlier in the day, in which he reportedly said he was "relieved" by Swiss franc weakness.
A finance ministry spokesman said Villiger had given an interview to a news agency, but he could not verify the contents of the interview.
